strengths: The benchmark addresses a genuine gap: existing RL-for-AFC benchmarks rely on external CFD solvers, are rarely differentiable, and lack MARL/3D support; FluidGym's fully differentiable, single-Python-stack design built on the GPU-accelerated PICT solver directly targets these limitations, and the comparison table (Table 1) against prior benchmarks is fair and informative.

Substantial engineering effort and resource commitment are evident (reportedly >16k GPU hours), with released environments, datasets, trained models, and a standardized train/val/test protocol with deterministic seeding—this materially improves reproducibility in a field criticized for inconsistent evaluation.

The appendix provides meaningful physical validation of the environments (grid refinement for RBC, comparison of Cd/Cl/Nusselt numbers against prior literature), which is often missing in benchmark papers and lends credibility to the simulations.

The paper covers useful additional analyses: performance profiles in the style of Agarwal et al. (2021), IQM reporting, policy transfer from 2D to 3D and across domain sizes, and a gradient-based D-MPC baseline demonstrating the value of differentiability.
The limitations section is candid and honest about seed counts, default hyperparameters, GPU-only execution, and the proof-of-concept nature of the D-MPC evaluation.
weaknesses: There is a significant inconsistency between the claimed scope of the experiments and what was actually run: the paper claims 'an extensive experimental study covering all FluidGym environments', yet Table 7 shows 0 GPU hours (i.e., no experiments) for numerous environments including all RBC2D-wide, RBC3D-wide, TCFSmall3D-bottom, TCFLarge3D-bottom, and the medium/hard Airfoil3D variants. Many of the 13 advertised environments are defined but never evaluated, weakening the central contribution as presented.

The algorithmic evaluation is thin for a benchmark paper: only PPO and SAC (and their MA- variants) with default SB3 hyperparameters, evaluated on 5 seeds (3 for expensive 3D tasks). The headline finding that SAC outperforms PPO is already well established in the AFC literature, so the experimental insights offer limited new understanding beyond confirming prior results on new environments.

Statistical robustness is limited: with 3-5 seeds and the acknowledged high variance of RL, several conclusions (e.g., MA-SAC vs. MA-PPO differences 'within confidence intervals', transfer results that are 'on par, slightly below') are not strongly supported. Some reported results are puzzling and unexamined, e.g., PPO achieving negative drag reduction (-4.7%) on CylinderJet3D-hard while SAC fails (-0.5%), which warrants analysis rather than tabulation.

The differentiability claim, a key selling point, is only exercised via a minimal D-MPC proof of concept on a single 2D environment (CylinderJet2D). No comparison with other differentiable simulation approaches or gradient-based methods (e.g., DPC, differentiable RL) is provided, so the practical benefit of end-to-end differentiability remains largely undemonstrated.

The 'first standalone, fully differentiable' claim is somewhat overstated given HydroGym's partial JAX-based differentiability and the existence of general PDE-control benchmarks; the positioning relies on a specific conjunction of desiderata.

Dependencies on components that are themselves unpublished or future-dated (the PICT solver, cited as Franz et al., 2026) complicate reproducibility of the underlying simulation stack, and CUDA-only execution restricts accessibility.

The scope is specialized: for the ICML audience, the contribution is primarily an engineering/platform effort with limited methodological novelty; the learning-science insights are modest (confirming SAC > PPO, plausible MARL coordination observations), so the paper's significance hinges almost entirely on community adoption of the benchmark, which is not yet evidenced.

strengths: FluidGym addresses a genuine and clearly documented gap: existing AFC benchmarks either depend on external CFD solvers, lack differentiability, or offer limited 3D/MARL support (Table 1 comparison is fair and well-researched). A standalone, fully differentiable PyTorch suite is a useful contribution to the RL-for-flow-control community.

The experimental study is substantial (over 25k GPU hours, Table 8), covers four flow classes across 2D/3D and difficulty levels, and uses evaluation methodology (IQM, performance profiles after Agarwal et al. 2021, stratified bootstrap CIs, per-step metrics) that is notably more rigorous than typical practice in this literature.

The paper demonstrates real use of the differentiability claim: DPC baseline experiments (Section 4.3) show ~1-2 orders of magnitude sample-efficiency gains over PPO/SAC, giving concrete evidence the benchmark enables gradient-based control research, not just classical RL.

Solver and environment validation against prior literature (cylinder drag within 3.84% of Rabault et al., RBC grid refinement study, airfoil lift/drag vs. Wang et al., TCF opposition control at ~20% drag reduction consistent with Guastoni et al.) supports physical correctness.
Excellent reproducibility posture: released environments, datasets, trained models, unified train/val/test splits with seeded RNG, full hyperparameter tables (Appendix D), and runtime benchmarks.

The transfer-learning studies (2D->3D, small->large TCF domain) are a genuinely interesting experimental component enabled by the benchmark's design and yield a non-obvious finding (small-domain MARL policies transfer well and outperform large-domain-trained policies).
Honest limitations section: authors acknowledge limited seeds, CUDA-only requirement, DPC restricted to 2D environments, and default hyperparameters.
weaknesses: Scientific novelty is primarily engineering and integration rather than new understanding; environment designs largely follow prior work (Vignon et al. 2023, Vasanth et al. 2024, Rabault et al. 2019, Suarez et al. 2025), and the core algorithmic findings (SAC competitive with or better than PPO) are modest and partly within confidence intervals, as the authors themselves note.

Only five random seeds are used, which the authors acknowledge limits statistical robustness of the central algorithmic comparisons; several headline conclusions (e.g., MA-SAC marginally higher than MA-PPO) rest on differences the paper admits lie within confidence intervals.

The claimed contribution of 'covering all core FluidGym environment classes and difficulty levels' is inconsistent with Table 8: all RBC2D-WIDE, RBC3D-WIDE, and *-BOTTOM variants show 0 GPU hours because they were 'not evaluated separately.' This coverage gap should be stated more prominently.

The min-max normalized scores used in the aggregate analysis (Figure 4) are normalized independently per environment-difficulty pair against the best-performing run, introducing a mild circularity: the top-performing algorithm partially defines the scale on which all algorithms are ranked.

Baseline evaluation uses default SB3 hyperparameters for comparability, but this handicaps conclusions about 'algorithmic performance'; the ablation addressing this covers only PPO network size on two environments, which is thin given the paper's claims about SAC vs. PPO.
The PPO device is set to CPU (Table 5) while SAC uses CUDA; this is unexplained and potentially confounds the runtime comparisons in Figure 9 and per-step runtime claims.

Gradient-based (DPC) evaluation is limited to two 2D environments, with training even degrading and stopping early on CylinderJet2D-easy; the claim that FluidGym establishes 'a scalable foundation for gradient-based learning' is therefore only weakly evidenced in 3D settings.

Incomplete coverage in key tables: 3D airfoil medium/hard results are missing for several algorithms, and one case uses four instead of five seeds, making the aggregate profiles uneven across environments.
